records.old: Does the light-dependent reaction run at night? What does this suggest about what the plant uses during the night to repair itself?'
records.new: Do the light-dependent reactions run at night? So where does the plant get its energy at night, and what do you think actually brings the wilted leaves back to normal?'
records.why: Q3 assumed the plant stores ATP and NADPH from the day and uses them to 'repair' itself at night, and the teacher notes said the light reactions are 'DARK-independent'. That is wrong: ATP and NADPH are used up within seconds to minutes and are not stored overnight. At night the light reactions stop; the plant gets energy by respiring the sugars and starch made in the day. The overnight recovery from wilting is a water-balance effect (stomata close, transpiration falls, roots keep taking up water, turgor returns), as Lesson 2 already explains, not a photosynthesis repair. The question is rewritten to lead to those three ideas. Checked against the standard textbook account: ATP/NADPH are short-lived carriers made only in light; respiration runs in the dark.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e, Photosynthesis unit (The Light-Dependent Reactions; The Calvin Cycle); Taiz, Zeiger, Moller & Murphy, Plant Physiology and Development (photosynthesis, mineral nutrition and plant water relations chapters)
records.group_headline: Lesson 5 said the plant stores ATP and NADPH in the day and uses them to repair itself at night; they are not stored, and overnight recovery from wilting is a water-balance effect

records.old: For Q3, say: 'This is a tricky one. I am going to give you 15 seconds to think silently before anyone speaks.' [Allow 15 seconds of WAIT TIME.] Then cold-call: 'Kipchoge — what do you think?' Guide learners toward the idea that the plant uses pre-formed ATP and NADPH (or synthesised sugars from the Calvin cycle) stored during daylight for overnight repair, and that the light reactions themselves are DARK-independent only in the sense that no light reactions run — but the products are already stored.
records.new: For Q1, expected answer: the oxygen comes from the splitting of water (photolysis) at Photosystem II, not from CO₂; a chemical that blocks photolysis would stop oxygen release and electron flow, so bubbles and ATP/NADPH would fall. If a learner says the oxygen comes from CO₂, ask: 'Look at your photolysis card: which molecule is split, and what comes off it?' For Q3, say: 'This is a tricky one. I am going to give you 15 seconds to think silently before anyone speaks.' [Allow 15 seconds of WAIT TIME.] Then cold-call: 'Kipchoge — what do you think?' Expected answers: (a) No, the light-dependent reactions stop in the dark, and ATP and NADPH are not stored for the night; (b) at night the plant gets energy by breaking down the sugars and starch it made during the day (respiration, studied in Sub-Strand 2.3); (c) the leaves recover because the stomata close, water loss falls and the roots keep taking up water, so turgor returns (Lesson 2). If a learner says the plant 'uses stored ATP', ask: 'Is ATP a store or a carrier that is used straight away? Which molecule is the real store?'
records.why: Replaces the incorrect Q3 guidance (see the group headline) and adds expected answers for Q1 and Q3 with an 'if students say X' move, which the lesson lacked.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e, Photosynthesis unit (The Light-Dependent Reactions; The Calvin Cycle); Taiz, Zeiger, Moller & Murphy, Plant Physiology and Development (photosynthesis, mineral nutrition and plant water relations chapters)

records.old: (A) Carbon dioxide — scientists at the University of Nairobi have measured CO2 concentrations inside and outside leaf chambers; CO2 enters through stomata as shown in Lesson 2. records.new: (A) Carbon dioxide — plant scientists measure CO2 concentrations inside and outside leaf chambers to show that CO2 enters through the stomata, as seen in Lesson 2. (B) Water — rain or irrigation water soaks into the soil and moves into the plant roots, up the xylem and into the mesophyll cells; water is one of the two substances that are turned into glucose and oxygen.
records.why: Two problems in the reading. (1) Water reaches the plant roots from rain, irrigation or soil water, not from municipal borehole supply, and a claim that University of Nairobi scientists measured leaf-chamber CO2 cannot be checked, so it is made general. (2) 'Stroma' is used before it is taught (Lesson 5), so it is replaced by plain wording. Checked against the standard account of water as a reactant (photolysis) and of CO2 entry via stomata.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e, Photosynthesis unit (The Light-Dependent Reactions; The Calvin Cycle) (Overview of Photosynthesis)

records.old: Build the word equation collaboratively, scribing exactly what learners say and correcting gently.
records.new: Build the word equation collaboratively, scribing exactly what learners say and correcting gently. Then name the difference: carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials (reactants), used up and turned into glucose and oxygen; light energy is the energy source and chlorophyll is the pigment that captures it, and neither is used up. If a learner says the plant 'eats' chlorophyll or soil, ask: 'Look at the equation — is chlorophyll on either side of it?'
records.why: The lesson calls light and chlorophyll 'raw materials' together with CO2 and water, which can leave learners thinking chlorophyll is used up (the lesson's own reflection names this misconception, but nothing in the lesson addresses it). The Final Explanation already expects learners to separate reactants from light and chlorophyll, so the lesson now teaches it, with an 'if students say X' move.

records.old: When the rate of water vapour loss through open stomata exceeds the rate at which xylem can deliver water from the roots, leaf cells lose turgor pressure and the plant wilts.
records.new: When the rate of water vapour loss through open stomata exceeds the rate at which xylem can deliver water from the roots, leaf cells lose turgor pressure and the plant wilts. records.old: The teacher uses a three-level rubric when marking: Emerging — learner describes observations without causal mechanisms or uses vocabulary incorrectly; Developing — learner provides partial causal chains for one or both phenomena with mostly correct vocabulary; Achieved — learner provides complete, accurate, causally connected explanations for both phenomena and makes a relevant, evidence-based connection to Kenyan agricultural practice. Learners who score Emerging are identified for targeted support in the following term. All learners receive written feedback within one week.
records.new: The teacher marks with the CBE levels. Exceeds Expectations: complete, accurate, causally connected explanations for both phenomena and a specific, evidence-based farming recommendation. Meets Expectations: correct causal chains for both phenomena (Part 1: strong light, open stomata, water vapour lost faster than xylem supplies it, turgor lost, recovery at night; Part 2: less light, less ATP and NADPH, less glucose, slow growth and less chlorophyll made) and a relevant Kenyan example. Approaches Expectations: a correct chain for one phenomenon or partial chains for both, with some vocabulary misused. Below Expectations: describes observations without a causal mechanism, or confuses wilting (water loss) with mineral deficiency. Learners who are Below Expectations are identified for targeted support in the following term. All learners receive written feedback within one week.
records.why: The task is the end-of-unit assessment but was marked with a three-level scheme (Emerging, Developing, Achieved), not the four CBE levels. It now uses Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations, and gives the teacher a look-for for each part (the expected answers already in the Summary Table) so a teacher who did not write the lesson can mark it.

value.criterion: Scientific accuracy of photosynthesis (reactants, light and chlorophyll, equations, two stages)
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly distinguishes the reactants from light energy and chlorophyll, gives both equations, and accurately describes where each stage occurs, the key steps and how ATP and NADPH link the stages.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States most requirements and equations correctly and describes both stages with minor omissions or errors.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Names some requirements or an equation but confuses the stages or leaves out key steps.

value.criterion: Explaining wilting using leaf structure and water movement
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly links stomata, transpiration, xylem supply rate and loss of turgor, explains why wet soil does not prevent wilting, and explains overnight recovery.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains wilting through water loss and turgor but is less clear about rate of loss versus supply or about recovery.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Says the plant lacks water or is hot without linking stomata, transpiration and turgor.

value.criterion: Use of evidence and limiting factors
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurately uses the starch test, the light-intensity graph shape, the temperature curve and the definition of a limiting factor to justify claims, and correctly applies them to the Naivasha and Kericho examples.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses some evidence and defines a limiting factor, with partial application to the farm examples.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States facts without evidence, or the limiting factor idea is missing or incorrect.

value.criterion: Integration of minerals and the complete causal chain for the pallor
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Builds a clear, sequenced chain from low light to less ATP and NADPH to less glucose to slow growth and less chlorophyll maintained, and explains the role of nitrogen and magnesium in chlorophyll.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives a mostly complete chain but one step or the link to chlorophyll or minerals is missing or unclear.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives a brief statement that shade means less food, without a causal chain.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses precise scientific vocabulary, organises answers clearly, and gives a sensible, evidence-based farming recommendation.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Mostly clear writing with some correct terms and a reasonable but general recommendation.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Writing is unclear or uses few scientific terms, and the recommendation is missing or not linked to the evidence.

records.why: The Final Explanation rubric uses the headings Excellent, Proficient and Developing. The CBE levels are Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations. The contract allows only three level fields and the printed headings are fixed, so the CBE level names are written at the start of each descriptor.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the data contract allows only three level fields, so a Below Expectations descriptor cannot be added to the Final Explanation. Teachers should mark work that does not reach 'Approaches' as Below Expectations; the Lesson 10 task already has all four levels in its marking notes.

The data says 'Strand 2.0: Physiology of Plants and Animals' and 'Sub-Strand 2.1: Plant Nutrition' (10 lessons). Numbers (2.0, 2.1) agree throughout; I did not rename anything.
